title: EVgo starts building Tesla Superchargers under license
gist: EVgo will begin deploying its own license-built Tesla V4 Superchargers on its US network this fall, becoming the first US company to build Tesla's charger design under license (following a similar UK license deployment in 2024), as Tesla increasingly leans on Supercharger licensing and network revenue while cutting car prices and burning cash on robotics and AI.

themes.theme: Tesla's Supercharger network opens to license-built hardware

insights.claim: EVgo will start deploying EVgo-made Tesla V4 Superchargers onto its US network later this fall, making it the first company to build license-manufactured Tesla Superchargers in the US; the first license-built Superchargers were deployed in the UK in 2024.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Tesla licensing its charger hardware design to a third-party operator (rather than only opening network access) is a distinct monetization channel — a template that could scale to other charging network operators and generate recurring licensing revenue for Tesla beyond direct network ownership.

insights.claim: The Tesla Supercharger network transitioned from a proprietary walled garden to an open one starting in 2023 when Tesla began opening it to other EVs, with Ford signing the first deal; by the following year the CCS1 plug, the prior non-Tesla charging standard, was 'living on borrowed time' as J3400/NACS became the de facto standard.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: This confirms NACS has effectively won the US EV charging standard war against CCS1, a multi-year competitive dynamic now reaching its endpoint with third-party licensed hardware manufacturing — relevant for EV charging equipment and connector supply chain investments.

insights.claim: The EVgo-built DC chargers can deliver up to 500 kW at up to 1,000 V and support both NACS and CCS1 plugs; the hardware will be owned and operated by EVgo, which will handle site host engagement, utility interconnection, and price management at EVgo Supercharger sites, while the chargers will appear in both Tesla's and EVgo's in-car navigation and apps.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: EVgo retaining ownership/operation while integrating into Tesla's navigation/routing ecosystem is a specific commercial structure (licensing + integration, not just a supply agreement) worth noting for how future EV charging network partnerships may be structured.

insights.claim: EVgo says the V4 Supercharger cables will be long enough to reach non-Tesla EVs regardless of charge port location, addressing a known problem where V3 charger cables have been too short for many non-Tesla EVs gaining Supercharger network access.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: This is a concrete engineering fix to a known friction point in Tesla's network-opening strategy, relevant to assessing how smoothly the broader NACS transition is proceeding for non-Tesla drivers.

insights.claim: The article notes Tesla is making less money selling more cars as it cuts prices to attract customers amid rising inflation and tariff costs each quarter, while simultaneously burning through revenue at 'an impressive rate' spending on robotics and AI — meaning Supercharger licensing fees and returns from deployed chargers are increasingly welcome revenue.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: This frames Supercharger network/licensing revenue as a growing offset to declining core-vehicle margins at Tesla, suggesting investors should track charging-network and licensing revenue as an increasingly material line item as vehicle margins compress under price cuts and tariffs.
